data.title: Humno – the earliest written mention of a Slavic farm building
data.excerpt: A humno is a farm building used mainly for storing harvested grain, hay or farm tools. Archaeologists have attested such buildings among the Slavs as early as the period after their arrival, and the word itself appears as gumno in a Great Moravian text, the Decrees of the Holy Fathers — the oldest known written record of the term.
data.metaTitle: Humno – the earliest mention of a Slavic building
data.metaDescription: The farm building known as a humno among the Slavs: attested by archaeologists soon after their arrival and named in a Great Moravian text of the 9th century.

children.text: Today the term HUMNO is understood to mean a farm building used mainly for storing harvested grain, hay or farm tools. Archaeologists have attested the construction of such buildings among the Slavs as early as the period after their arrival in the territory of present-day Slovakia. Few people know, however, that in the 9th century our Slavic ancestors used precisely the word “HUMNO” to denote this type of building.

We have in fact found proof of the earliest use of the word “HUMNO” in a text whose origin goes back to the period of Great Moravia. It is the work “Ustanovenia svätých otcov o pokání za vraždu a o každom hriechu” (Decrees of the Holy Fathers on penance for murder and for every sin).
In point 27 of the decrees the following provision can be found:

blocks.text: If anyone sets fire to a house or to a humno, let him do penance for seven years, on bread and water.

children.text:
The Decrees of the Holy Fathers came into being as a translation from Latin penitentials. These were used in their original form in Great Moravia even before the arrival of the Byzantine mission. They were a basic aid prescribed by canon law. The text was translated by someone from among Methodius's disciples who had a good command of Latin. Gorazd and Clement are possible candidates, but this is only a hypothesis. It is also possible that the Decrees come directly from Constantine the Philosopher. The text has survived in the manuscript (Glagolitic) Euchologium sinaiticum of Macedonian origin from the 11th century, and then in two later copies (in Cyrillic) in Old Russian manuscripts (the Ustjužskaja kormčaja kniga from the end of the 13th century and the Joasafskaja kormčaja kniga from the 16th century).

The text has also preserved passages of the gospel, including elements of the Great Moravian language. From a linguistic point of view, the most striking feature is the abundant use of participles in a substantival sense and in determinative syntagmas – the author used this device in order to make the text of the legal provisions shorter and denser. (Source: Wikipedia)
